patient.history_present_illness: This 52-year-old right-handed African-American man, a high school principal with a history of excised cutaneous melanoma, presents to the neurology service for evaluation of progressive headaches and cognitive changes over the past seven weeks. His spouse is the primary historian and prompted this evaluation after the patient minimized his symptoms. Approximately seven weeks ago he began experiencing persistent right-sided headaches, which he described as a pressure sensation rather than pulsatile pain, prominent upon awakening in the morning and exacerbated by leaning forward. Acetaminophen provided partial relief. Over the ensuing four weeks, his spouse began noticing behavioral and cognitive changes that were distinctly out of character: he twice missed administrative meetings he himself had scheduled, repeatedly asked the same questions within a few minutes, left his school office unlocked on three occasions — something he had never done in 18 years as principal — and had difficulty composing a formal letter that would previously have taken him minutes. He was seen by his primary care physician approximately five weeks ago who attributed symptoms to work stress. Ten days prior to the current presentation, his spouse witnessed an episode in which the patient abruptly stopped mid-sentence during dinner, stared blankly with a slightly glassy expression for approximately 15 seconds, then resumed conversation. He appeared unaware of the interruption and denied any subjective experience. There was no convulsive activity, loss of consciousness, or post-event confusion. This episode prompted urgent neurological referral. He denies fever, chills, night sweats, unexplained weight loss, or changes in skin lesions. Of substantial clinical concern is his history of cutaneous melanoma of the right posterior shoulder, resected three years ago with confirmed negative sentinel lymph node. The patient completed the recommended five-year surveillance protocol; his last dermatological examination five months ago was unremarkable, and a PET-CT performed eleven months ago revealed no evidence of metastatic disease. His current medications are amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, and low-dose aspirin. He is a former smoker with a 12-pack-year history, quit 15 years ago. He drinks alcohol occasionally. He sleeps with CPAP for obstructive sleep apnea.

mri.impression: Three distinct enhancing intracranial lesions: (1) a dominant ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis and restricted diffusion at the rim in the right parieto-occipital lobe (4.8 cm) with extensive FLAIR signal exceeding the enhancing boundary and midline shift; (2) a nodularly enhancing lesion in the right frontal white matter (1.9 cm); (3) a small ring-enhancing lesion at the left superior temporal gray-white junction (1.2 cm). The imaging differential includes multicentric/multifocal primary glioma and brain metastases; the gray-white junction location of the left temporal lesion and nodular enhancement of the right frontal lesion favor metastases, while the extensive FLAIR infiltration beyond the dominant lesion and irregular ring enhancement with internal septations are more consistent with a high-grade primary glial neoplasm. Primary CNS lymphoma is less likely given the peripheral rim restriction and heterogeneous enhancement pattern. Tissue diagnosis is required for definitive characterization. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: Differentiating multicentric glioblastoma from multiple brain metastases: the role of advanced MRI
results.key_finding: Multicentric GBM accounts for 2-5% of GBM cases and is the most common pattern of multifocal high-grade glioma. Key imaging features favoring multicentric GBM over metastases: (1) FLAIR infiltration extending beyond the enhancing lesion (particularly in the perilesional tissue, which appears as vasogenic edema around metastases), (2) elevated rCBV in perilesional FLAIR-abnormal tissue (rCBV ratio >1.75), which is typically normal in metastatic vasogenic edema, (3) elevated choline in non-enhancing perilesional tissue on MR spectroscopy. Gray-white junction location and homogeneous nodular enhancement favor metastasis.

results.title: WHO 2021 classification of CNS tumors: implications for clinical practice
results.key_finding: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4 is defined by IDH-wildtype status plus either microvascular proliferation or necrosis on histology, or by the presence of TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, or +7/-10 chromosomal signature. The WHO 2021 classification mandates integrated histomolecular diagnosis; imaging-based grading cannot substitute for tissue diagnosis with molecular profiling.

results.title: Multicentric versus multifocal glioblastoma: prognostic and management implications
results.key_finding: True multicentric GBM (lesions in anatomically distinct, non-contiguous brain regions without visible tract-based connectivity) carries a worse prognosis than unifocal GBM due to limited surgical options. Tissue biopsy of at least the dominant lesion is mandatory for integrated molecular diagnosis. Surgical cytoreduction of the dominant lesion may still be feasible and associated with survival benefit in selected patients.

output.summary: Multicentric GBM presents as multiple spatially distinct enhancing lesions and is frequently misdiagnosed as brain metastases, particularly when a prior malignancy is known. Advanced MRI techniques are critical for differentiation: elevated rCBV in perilesional non-enhancing tissue and metabolic abnormalities on MR spectroscopy extending into the FLAIR zone favor primary glioma over metastasis. However, tissue diagnosis with molecular profiling remains mandatory for definitive classification per WHO 2021 guidelines, which define GBM, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4 by integrated histomolecular criteria.

Multifocal enhancing lesions in a patient with a prior malignancy; staging CT negative for extracranial primary; perilesional MR perfusion and spectroscopy features favor infiltrating primary glioma over metastasis

PCNSL more typically presents as homogeneously enhancing, periventricular lesions with solid diffusion restriction and minimal surrounding edema in immunocompetent patients; ring enhancement with necrosis and extensive perilesional FLAIR infiltration are atypical

critical_actions: Obtain MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol) as the first step to characterize the multifocal lesions and define biopsy target
Initiate dexamethasone (e.g., 8 mg IV loading then 4 mg IV every 6 hours) to reduce symptomatic peritumoral edema and mass effect
Obtain urgent neurosurgical and neuro-oncology consultation for tissue diagnosis by stereotactic biopsy of the dominant lesion
Perform systemic staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast to exclude active extracranial primary malignancy before diagnosing primary brain tumor
Order pre-operative labs (CBC, CMP, coagulation, type and screen) before any surgical intervention
Include melanoma immunomarkers (Melan-A, HMB-45, SOX10) in the surgical pathology panel to definitively exclude melanoma metastasis
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform lumbar puncture given 6 mm midline shift and effacement of the right occipital horn — herniation risk
Do not diagnose brain metastases and initiate whole-brain radiotherapy or systemic melanoma therapy without tissue confirmation
Do not initiate tumor-directed therapy (temozolomide, immunotherapy) before histomolecular tissue diagnosis is established
key_reasoning_points: Multicentric GBM (multiple spatially non-contiguous enhancing lesions) accounts for 2-5% of GBM cases and is the most common high-grade glioma mimic of brain metastases; prior malignancy history dramatically increases anchoring bias toward metastatic disease

The critical imaging discriminator between multicentric GBM and multiple metastases is the perilesional non-enhancing tissue: in GBM this zone contains infiltrating tumor (elevated rCBV > 1.75, elevated choline on MRS), whereas metastatic edema is purely vasogenic (normal perilesional rCBV, no metabolic abnormality on MRS)

Elevated LDH and S100B are non-specific tumor markers that cannot distinguish between melanoma metastases and primary glioma; they should not independently drive the diagnosis toward metastatic disease
Staging CT and tissue melanoma immunomarkers (Melan-A, HMB-45) are required to actively exclude melanoma metastasis — surveillance negativity 11 months prior does not eliminate the possibility
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated in this case due to demonstrated mass effect (6 mm midline shift); do not perform LP even if CSF cytology for melanoma is considered
Tissue diagnosis with full WHO 2021 molecular profiling (IDH, MGMT, TERT, EGFR, +7/-10) is mandatory; imaging alone — including advanced MRI — cannot substitute for histomolecular classification

red_herrings.data_point: Prior cutaneous melanoma (pT2aN0M0), excised 3 years ago with negative sentinel lymph node
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors clinician toward brain metastases from prior melanoma; may prompt empiric melanoma systemic treatment or whole-brain radiotherapy without tissue confirmation
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Melanoma was pT2aN0M0 (low-intermediate risk) resected 3 years ago with most recent PET-CT 11 months ago negative; tissue biopsy with melanoma immunomarkers is required to confirm or exclude metastatic melanoma before any diagnosis is accepted

red_herrings.data_point: Elevated LDH (312 U/L) and S100B (0.18 µg/L) on initial labs
red_herrings.intended_effect: LDH elevation and detectable S100B in a patient with prior melanoma may be interpreted as tumor markers supporting metastatic melanoma recurrence
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: LDH and S100B are non-specific; LDH is elevated in many primary brain tumors including GBM; S100B positivity reflects active glial pathology (S100B is expressed by astrocytes and Schwann cells) and is not specific for melanoma; tissue diagnosis with specific immunomarkers (Melan-A, HMB-45) is required

red_herrings.data_point: Small indeterminate hepatic lesion (1.3 cm, segment 6) on staging CT
red_herrings.intended_effect: An indeterminate liver lesion in a patient with known prior melanoma and multifocal brain lesions may be interpreted as confirming systemic metastatic disease, reinforcing a misdiagnosis of metastatic melanoma
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The hepatic lesion is too small to characterize on CT and more likely represents a benign cyst or hemangioma; the staging CT otherwise shows no evidence of active systemic malignancy; MRI liver for further characterization is appropriate but this finding does not establish systemic melanoma recurrence
